cells.tense: You're here with it, and the care you give keeps going without needing a reason to.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you're growing and give someone the plain update on it today — what's working, what isn't. That hands you a straight look at what your care has been building, rather than the summary you keep for yourself, and it puts you beside the thing instead of watching it from across the room.
cells.core:
You're keeping something alive and the keeping has become ordinary — the water you don't forget, the small check you make without deciding to, the way you spot what's shifted since last week. Not forced and not dramatic. When this goes well it looks unglamorous and reliable from the outside: showing up on the plain days and letting that be enough, the same week after week, with nothing much to show for it that anyone else would notice.

There's more room in it than you're using. Describing the real state of it to one person — not the highlights, the actual state — is how you find out what's there. You may learn it's further along than the last time you reported on it, and saying so is a way of standing next to your own work rather than narrating it from a distance.
cells.sheetLine: You're keeping something alive with steady hands, and you know it.
cells.verb: keeping a thing alive on patience and small ordinary acts, long after the first spark has faded
cells.place: in the patch of life where something is still small enough to need regular tending

cells.tense: You're already out at next season's result, and the thing in front of you is being pulled toward it.
cells.ask: Before you adjust the plan again, write down only what's true of it right now — its size, its condition, nothing projected. That gives you back the real thing to care for, instead of the one you're arguing into being, and it lets you find out what's actually there rather than what you've decided should be.
cells.core:
You can see what this turns into and you're working backward from it — feeding, adjusting, nudging so it lands on schedule. The picture's real, and a picture isn't the plant. When something small is genuinely coming along, the care is mostly patient attention and time; the shape arrives on its own, with you there mainly to notice it and leave it be, and the calendar is the last thing it needs.

Pulling hard at a growing thing can bend it out of its own shape. The outcome you're holding so tightly is doing some of the work for you and some of it against you, and from where you're standing the two are hard to tell apart until you write down what's actually there.
cells.sheetLine: You're tending the harvest, not the thing in front of you.

cells.tense: The care you used to bring here has gone quiet, and you're standing well past where you set it down.
cells.ask: Choose the smallest living thing you've stepped back from and give it fifteen unhurried minutes today — no plan, no fixing, just look at it. That's one try, unforced, and it tells you whether there's anything left here you'd want to pick back up.
cells.core:
There's something you were looking after that you've stopped looking after. You can still name it — it hasn't disappeared — but your attention has worn thin, and walking past it has become easy. When care for a growing thing is going well, it looks like showing up on the ordinary days and letting that be enough, week after week, without anything loud to show for it and without anyone asking.

This isn't about summoning a feeling. It's one small physical act, once, and seeing what it stirs. The quiet doesn't have to be permanent, and a single try will tell you more than another year of leaving it untouched.
cells.sheetLine: You stopped reaching toward it, and you're not sure you want back in.

cells.tense: You're already the one keeping it going — the pen is moving — you just don't call it yours.
cells.ask: Name one thing you're holding together right now, and say out loud to someone that you're the one holding it. That returns your own effort in your own voice, where it can be seen, instead of running on quietly and uncredited.
cells.core:
The small repairs, the checking, the steady watering — you're doing all of it. And you describe the thing as simply surviving on its own. It isn't. It's surviving because you keep at it. When this goes well, the work tends to sink into the background: care stops being a decision and just becomes what happens, so the person doing it drops out of the frame entirely, and everyone, including you, starts calling it the thing's own momentum.

Saying who's doing the work isn't claiming credit you haven't earned. It's a plain word for what's already true, and it's been missing from how you tell it. Say it once to someone and hear how it lands.
cells.sheetLine: You're the one keeping it alive, and it's time that got said.
